title: Small groups
hookLine: Wesley's class meetings asked one question: how is it with your soul?
carry: how is it with your soul?
last: YOU WEREN'T MEANT TO DO IT ALONE.

lines: HOW IS IT WITH YOUR SOUL?
cards: Good, busy. It's so quick it barely counts as a question. Now step into a room of about a dozen people, farmers, miners, maids, shopkeepers, in eighteenth-century England, meeting on a weeknight.
A leader goes around the circle and asks each person the same question. Not how are you. Not how's work.
How is it with your soul? And each person has to answer. Honestly.

teach.b: Bristol, England, 1742. The Methodists, the movement led by John Wesley, owe money on their new meeting house.
Someone suggests a practical fix: divide the members into groups of about twelve, and have a leader collect a penny a week from each.
But the leaders, going door to door for their pennies, keep finding things out: a man drinking again, a family that can't eat. Wesley saw what was happening and made it the heart of the movement.
The class meeting was born. Once a week, each class met with its leader. They sang, they prayed, and the leader asked each one about their life with God.
The question tradition remembers them by is today's line: how is it with your soul? The classes could do something a sermon couldn't. You can hide in a crowd of a thousand.

teach.h: YOU CAN'T HIDE IN A CIRCLE OF TWELVE.
teach.b: You can't hide in a circle of twelve people who know your name. Jesus had said something that makes small numbers matter.
In the King James Bible: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three is enough.
The idea has spread far beyond Methodism: home groups, cell groups, Bible studies around kitchen tables, Catholic small faith communities.
All of them share the same bet: people change less from being taught at and more from being known.

teach.h: WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED.

how: Many Christians belong to a small group that meets weekly in a home or at church to read the Bible, pray and talk honestly about their lives; Methodist class meetings and their question 'how is it with your soul?' are one historic model.

o: a class where children learn Bible stories
a small church with fewer than fifty members
a dozen or so people who meet weekly, known by name

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a penny a week to pay a debt
asked each person about their soul

s: Wesley's class meetings began as a way to raise money
a penny a week each, to pay off the debt on a meeting house.
small groups are a modern invention of megachurches
Wesley's classes date to 1742, and Christians met in homes from the start.
class members could stay quiet and just listen
the leader asked each person about their soul, every week.

games.q: you're a Methodist class leader in 1742, sent to collect pennies. at one house you find a family that can't afford to eat. what do you do?
o: collect the penny anyway: rules are rules.
tell Wesley, and start caring for the people, not just the pennies.
games.why: the leaders kept finding out about people's lives, and Wesley turned the collection into the class meeting: weekly, honest care.

practice: Ask the question of yourself first: how is it with your soul, not your calendar or your inbox, your soul, whatever that word means to you right now.

Let the honest answer come, even if it's tired, or muddled, or better than you expected. Then think of one person you could really ask, someone who'd get past fine if they knew you meant it, and if you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Small groups. A dozen people, meeting weekly, known by name. Wesley's class meetings turned a penny collection into honest care.

carryVoice: Your line: how is it with your soul? Fine is allowed, but it isn't the whole answer. Until next time.
